readerTitle: Everyone said yes. That's why the plan failed.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (리모델링 회사, 회계·기장 서비스 회사) + 실제 기업 (Amazon 리더십 원칙, Bezos 2016 주주 서한)
insight: 반대는 결정 전에 분명히 말하고, 결정 뒤에는 온전히 실행해야 한다. 반쯤 실행한 계획은 아이디어가 틀렸는지조차 알려주지 않는다.
misconception: 회의에서 고개를 끄덕이고 속으로만 반대하는 것이 팀워크다. 결정에 동의하지 않으면 끝까지 맞서거나 조용히 따르는 수밖에 없다.

sources.text: Amazon Leadership Principles: "Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit"
Bezos, J. (2017). 2016 Letter to Shareholders, Amazon (Amazon Studios 사례)
리모델링 회사와 기장 서비스 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Amazon 리더십 원칙의 정확한 명칭("Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit")과 설명 문구(도전하고, 결정 후에는 전적으로 헌신)를 게시 직전 Amazon 공식 페이지에서 다시 확인하세요.
Bezos 2016 주주 서한(2017년 4월 공개)에서 Amazon Studios 오리지널 작품에 대해 본인은 회의적이었지만 "disagree and commit"하고 팀을 진행시켰다는 내용을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 직접 인용 없이 요약만 적었습니다.
이 표현의 기원은 Intel(Andy Grove), Sun Microsystems 등으로 거론되지만 확실하지 않아 카드에는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Everyone said yes. That's why the plan failed.
body: A home renovation company wants to try fixed-price quotes instead of billing by the hour. In the meeting, every estimator nods.
Three months later, the trial has failed. Fewer clients said yes, and the idea is dropped.
The twist: nobody ever really tried it.

image.label: A meeting where everyone nods while crossing their fingers under the table
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 회의 테이블 위로는 모두 고개를 끄덕이며 웃고 있고, 테이블 아래로는 손가락을 꼬거나 팔짱을 낀 손이 보임. 리모델링 회사 분위기(도면, 줄자). 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: You think the new plan is a mistake.
body: You're the lead estimator. You worry fixed prices will hurt the firm on messy jobs, like old houses with hidden wiring problems.
The owner asks for final thoughts before deciding. What do you do?

options.text: Stay quiet. The owner has clearly made up their mind
options.feedback: You keep the peace today. But the owner never hears the risk you saw, and your doubts tend to leak into the work later.

options.text: Make your case clearly, then back whatever is decided
options.feedback: The owner gets your best argument while it can still change the decision, and the plan gets your full effort either way.

options.text: Push hard, and don't sign on until the owner changes course
options.feedback: Your concern gets heard. But if the owner still says yes, the team now runs a plan its lead estimator refuses to back.

cards.title: The test measured doubt, not the idea.
body: The estimators nodded, but kept their doubts. They padded fixed quotes "to be safe." They sent them days later than hourly quotes. When clients asked, they shrugged that the owner was "trying something new."
Fewer clients signed. The owner concluded fixed pricing doesn't work.
But the firm never learned whether it does. A plan done halfway fails more often, and it hides why it failed.

cards.title: Disagree and commit
body: **Disagree and commit** means two things in order. Before a decision, you argue openly for what you believe. After it, you carry it out fully, as if it were your own idea.
The opposite is common: agree in the room, resist in the work. That gives you the worst of both. The decision-maker misses your warning, and the plan gets weak effort.

image.label: A path that splits into 'argue' before a decision point and 'all in' after it
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. 가운데 "Decision" 깃발. 왼쪽 구간은 여러 색 말풍선이 부딪히는 "Disagree", 오른쪽 구간은 모두 같은 방향으로 함께 노를 젓는 "Commit". 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.

cards.softwareNote: An engineer who argued against a feature can still build it well and suggest the usage number that would show it isn't working. A feature shipped grudgingly tells you nothing about whether users wanted it.

cards.title: Amazon wrote it into its principles.
body: The phrase became widely known through Amazon. One of its leadership principles is "Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit." It asks people to challenge decisions, even when that's uncomfortable, and then commit wholly once the call is made.

In his 2016 letter to shareholders, Jeff Bezos said it applies to bosses too. He described a show from Amazon Studios that he doubted. The team believed in it, so he told them he disagreed but would commit, and let them go ahead.

cards.title: Commit without pretending.
body: Committing is easier when the way out is agreed in advance. You don't have to fake belief. You just have to give the plan a fair chance.

breakdown.label: Disagree openly
breakdown.detail: Put your strongest case on the table

breakdown.label: One person decides
breakdown.detail: Be clear who owns the call

breakdown.label: Commit fully
breakdown.detail: Do the work as if it were your idea

breakdown.label: Review on a set date
breakdown.detail: Agree up front what result would change the plan

cards.title: It is not "agree or else."
body: The idea only works if disagreement is truly welcome before the decision. If a boss uses "disagree and commit" to shut down debate, it becomes plain obedience.
It also has a hard limit. Don't commit to something unsafe, illegal or dishonest. Those concerns get escalated, not swallowed.
And for big decisions you can't undo, slow down and hear every objection first. Commitment is cheapest when the decision can be reversed.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: You manage client accounts. The director moved all new-client onboarding to an online portal. You argued for keeping email, since older clients struggle with logins. You lost. The team agreed to review the change in 60 days.
Two weeks in, a long-time client calls, frustrated with the portal. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the client honestly that you didn't want the portal either
options.feedback: It feels honest, but it tells the client your firm is divided. It also makes the portal fail faster, for reasons that have nothing to do with the portal.

options.text: Help them through it, log the problem, and bring every such case to the 60-day review
options.feedback: The client gets help, the plan gets a fair test, and your concern comes back with evidence instead of opinion.

options.text: Ask the director to reverse the decision now
options.feedback: Fair if something serious and unexpected happened. But one frustrated client is the risk you already raised, not new information.

cards.title: Argue before. Commit after. Review on schedule.
body: A plan done halfway can't tell you whether the idea was wrong. Say your doubts out loud, then give the decision your full effort.
**Try it today:** think of one decision you went along with but never fully backed. Either commit to it properly this week, or ask for a review date and the result that would change it.
